<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and executed the Q&A format cleanly, but the decisive clash centered on the rigidity of B's proposed "standing floor," defined as bending only for an "equivalent existential threat." A's pressure question forced B to commit to that threshold, and A's closing turned it into a genuine liability: a rigid floor forecloses preventive reallocation to allies facing serious but sub-existential danger, which is precisely the opportunity-cost tradeoff the motion asks debaters to weigh. B never squarely answered why prevention should be discounted, instead reasserting that rigidity is "the point." B's strongest counter-move—quoting A's concession in [A4.3] that signals "cannot eliminate uncertainty" as "fatal"—was rhetorically sharp but selectively read; A's closing restored the comparative frame by noting a standing pledge is equally doubtable and that concrete reinforcement is a more observable signal than an abstract promise. A also more directly answered the motion's explicit "even if it reduces resources for other priorities" framing by keeping the opportunity-cost mechanics concrete (interceptors, ammunition, allied air defense), while B's deterrence-signaling and alliance-cohesion arguments, though elegant, rested more on asserted adversary psychology than demonstrated mechanism. This makes A's path to victory slightly cleaner and more resilient after the full exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing turning B's own "equivalent existential threat" threshold (from B4.1) into a liability—arguing it discounts legitimate preventive reallocation—was the most damaging unresolved point, since B never explained why sub-existential but urgent competing needs should lose automatically.</best_rebuttal>
